# Welcome

## Who we are

Centre for the Mathematical Modelling of Infectious Diseases

London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

::: {.fragment}
The course was built by [several people](../../authors.qmd) over more than a decade, and this year it is taught in Julia for the first time.
:::

## Who you are

A quick round of the room:

- your name
- where you work, and on what
- one thing you would like to be able to do by Thursday afternoon

::: {.fragment}
We will come back to that last one on Thursday.
:::

## What this course is about

Fitting *mechanistic* models to infectious disease data.

::: {.fragment}
You have a model of how an epidemic works.
You have data from one that happened.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Neither tells you the parameters. Getting from one to the other is the subject.
:::

## What you need

You need to have programmed before, in R, Python or something similar.

::: {.fragment}
You do not need to have written any Julia. The course teaches what it uses, and every line of code is given complete.
:::

::: {.fragment}
You do not need to remember any statistics you have forgotten. We build the inference up from likelihoods and Bayes' rule.
:::

# The four days

## Where we are going

| Day | Question |
|---|---|
| Monday | How do you fit a deterministic model, and why is it hard? |
| Tuesday | Did it work, and does the model make sense? |
| Wednesday | What if the epidemic itself is random? |
| Thursday | What if you cannot write the likelihood at all? |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

## Monday: fitting

The likelihood, priors, and Metropolis-Hastings by hand before we let a sampler do it.

::: {.fragment}
By this evening you will have fitted an epidemic model to data with code you wrote yourself.
:::

## Tuesday: trusting the fit

A chain that has run is not a chain that has converged, and a model that fits is not a model that is right.

::: {.fragment}
Diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, and the Tristan da Cunha outbreak, which we use for the rest of the week.
:::

## Wednesday: stochastic models

Real epidemics in small populations are not smooth curves.

::: {.fragment}
Once the model is stochastic the likelihood stops being available, and particle filters are how we get it back.
:::

## Thursday: giving up on the likelihood

Approximate Bayesian computation asks only that you can simulate.

::: {.fragment}
Then we put every method side by side and ask which one *your* problem needs.
:::

# How it runs

## The shape of a session

Each session is a short set of slides, then a practical you work through.

::: {.fragment}
The practicals are the course. The slides exist to get you into them.
:::

## The exercises

Every exercise is about the *inference*, never about getting the code to run.

::: {.fragment}
You will be asked to predict what a cell prints before running it, to read a diagnostic, to work out why a fit failed, and to choose between two options and defend it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Every one has a worked answer. Open it once you have had a go.
:::

## Working together

Sit with someone. Compare answers, especially where you disagree.

::: {.fragment}
Ask us anything at any point. If you are stuck for five minutes, that is already too long.
:::

## Practicalities

- 09:30–12:30 and 13:30–17:00, with a break in each block
- Thursday is a half day
- The afternoon break is a good moment to go outside

::: {.fragment}
Everything is online and stays online, including after the course.
:::
